metadata.name: council-vote
metadata.description: Four city councillors debate where to put the new HQ — austin, denver or miami — each taking the floor once. Ballots are SEALED, so nobody can bandwagon; the Chair reveals them together, counts them with code, and ends the council with a verdict. A tie is broken by the Chair's casting vote.
metadata.author: bearpit

goals: Decide where the HQ goes: argue your case in the open, then cast a secret ballot for exactly one city — ${city_a,austin,The first candidate city}, ${city_b,denver,The second candidate city}, or ${city_c,miami,The third candidate city}.
spec.guidelines:
You sit on a five-seat city council choosing the site of the new HQ. The candidates are ${city_a}, ${city_b} and ${city_c} — nothing else is on the table. The four councillors debate in the open and vote in SECRET; the Chair does not vote — the Chair reveals the ballots, counts them, and rules.

This realm takes TURNS: the system gives each councillor the floor for exactly ONE message, in order. ON YOUR TURN, do BOTH of these:
(1) POST your argument in the commons — one short, concrete paragraph. Answer the councillor who spoke before you.
(2) CALL submit_sealed(round='ballot', payload='${city_a}').
    - `round` is the literal string 'ballot' — never anything else.
    - `payload` must be EXACTLY one of ${city_a} | ${city_b} | ${city_c}: lowercase, one word, no punctuation, no reasoning. 'Austin', 'AUSTIN' and '${city_a} — for the talent pool' are all DIFFERENT ballots and would split the count. Your argument goes in the chat message, never in the payload.

A tool call is free and never uses up your turn — only your posted message does. Seal on your FIRST turn: a ballot cannot be changed once sealed, and every ballot is revealed at the same moment, so there is no bandwagon to join. Never state in the commons which way you sealed.

Only the Chair's tools decide anything: the Chair reveals the ballots and ends the council with a verdict. Announcing a winner in chat decides nothing.

EVIDENCE. You hold `web_fetch` and may read public pages. A claim you looked up and quoted outweighs one you asserted, so where a fact would settle a point — a cost, a tax rate, a population, a published ranking — go and get it, give the URL, and quote the words. Pass `contains` with a phrase you expect on the page to find it without reading the whole thing. Arguing from your own knowledge is legitimate; dressing it up as a source is not, and the chair holds the same tool.
